[Everyday Tonality 6](tagg-loops.qmd) follows Philip Tagg's chapters on chord loops. The YouTube channel
12tone has its own theory of loops, tested in the video *I Listened To 500 Songs To Prove A Point*. This page
puts the two side by side. Press ▶ to hear a loop on the band, one chord a bar.

## What a loop is

**Tagg:** a loop is a cycle of usually three or four chords, repeated, lasting about 3 to 8 seconds; longer
cycles such as the twelve-bar blues are not loops (pp. 411, 419). A turnaround can use the same chords; the
difference is its job, sending the section back to the start.

**12tone:** a progression takes you through a series of places; a loop *is* the place. You hear the whole loop
as one thing that turns round, so you see it from different sides. That is why, in *Fast Car*, Tracy Chapman can
sing B over an F♯ chord and A over E without it sounding like a clash: the melody fits the loop, not each chord.

**Both** count a loop in four slots. 12tone splits a loop into four roughly equal stretches of time: a
three-chord loop has one chord twice as long (two "chords" that sound the same), and a five-chord loop squeezes
two chords into one slot. Tagg notes the same thing: in a three-chord loop the medial and incoming chord are
usually the same chord, as in *La Bamba*'s I–IV–V–V (p. 415).

## Naming the chords in a loop

**Tagg** replaces "dominant" and "subdominant", which he finds misleading outside classical harmony, with names
for a chord's *place* in the loop (pp. 414–415):

- **outgoing** chord: the first change away from I;
- **medial** chord: the middle;
- **incoming** chord: the last before I comes round again (and the **turnaround** chord when it leads back).

In the vamp I–vi–ii–V, vi is outgoing, ii medial, V incoming and turnaround. I is "both starting point and
destination of the loop".

**12tone** names a chord by *how it moves*, not by its place or by any key. First the motion between two chords:

- **strong**: by a fifth (up or down) or by a step (whole or half, up or down);
- **weak**: anything else, usually a third; staying on the same chord counts as weak too.

Then each chord by its way in and way out:

| In | Out | Function | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| weak | weak | **island** | a little side trip |
| strong | strong | **connector** | pushes on to the next chord |
| weak | strong | **signpost** | starts a chain of resolutions |
| strong | weak | **destination** | ends the chain: a sort of stop |

The **loop shape** is the mix of strong and weak motion (contour) and where the destinations fall (anchoring).

## The same loops, both ways

Tagg's loops from chapters 13–14, worked out in 12tone's terms (in C; the analysis is this site's, applying
12tone's rules):

| Loop | Tagg | Motions | 12tone functions | Shape |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [▶]{.tg-play data-chords="C Am Dm G"} I–vi–ii–V | the vamp | weak, strong, strong, strong | destination, signpost, connector, connector | **cascade**, anchored on 1 |
| [▶]{.tg-play data-chords="C Am F G"} I–vi–IV–V | the 1950s–60s teen-pop loop | weak, weak, strong, strong | destination, island, signpost, connector | **disc**, anchored on 1 |
| [▶]{.tg-play data-chords="C F G G"} I–IV–V–V | the *La Bamba* loop | strong, strong, weak, strong | connector, connector, destination, signpost | **cascade**, anchored on 3 |
| [▶]{.tg-play data-chords="C G Am F"} I–V–vi–IV | (an ionian loop) | strong, strong, weak, strong | connector, connector, destination, signpost | **cascade**, anchored on 3 |

"Motions" are the changes 1→2, 2→3, 3→4 and 4→back to 1. A **cascade** has a signpost, a destination and two
connectors; a **disc** (Destination, Island, Signpost, Connector) swaps one connector for an island. 12tone calls
the disc "a more classic shape, popular in the doo-wop era", which is the same music Tagg finds the I–vi–IV–V loop
in. Tagg's "the tonic is the destination" agrees with 12tone here too: in the vamp, I is the destination chord.

## Where they differ

- **Home chord.** Tagg's names need a home chord (I). Much of his chapter 14 is about finding it: the same
  chords can be ionian or mixolydian, and the lead-in (anacrusis) is the best clue. 12tone's functions do not use a
  key at all, so a loop gets the same shape whichever chord you call home.
- **History or shape.** Tagg asks where a loop comes from (jazz vamps, teen pop, rock'n'roll's twelve-bar and
  V–IV–I) and groups loops by mode. 12tone asks what a loop does: how much it pushes forward, and where it rests.
- **Evidence.** Tagg's tables list recordings that use each loop. 12tone counted: 500 songs, ten picked at random
  each year from the Billboard year-end top 100, 1976–2025.

## 12tone's survey

What he predicted, and what he found (his own counts, as he gives them in the video):

- 234 of the 500 songs had a loop somewhere; about a quarter were one loop all the way through, more in the
  last 25 years.
- **Balanced** loops (at least one connector and one destination) 71%, **extreme** loops (all connectors, or
  signposts and destinations taking turns) 22%, **subdued** loops (more than one island) 7%. About two thirds of
  the balanced loops were cascades.
- Destinations by position: 1 = 100, 3 = 64, 4 = 48, 2 = 32, as he predicted (position 1 most, 2 least). Many of
  the position-2 loops came from EDM-flavoured songs of the early 2010s.
- Two chords in one slot: 38 cases; 35 moved strongly inside the slot, 33 were signposts or connectors.

His caveats: one listener, 500 songs, and only chart hits, so the charts' biases come with it.

## Songs he plays

These are in the [Tune Directory](../practice/tune-directory.qmd) with a link to the video (the transcript has
no times, so the link goes to the start):

- *Fast Car* (Tracy Chapman): melody and loop.
- *Special Lady* (Ray, Goodman & Brown): strong motion by fifths, a II–V–I.
- *Scream & Shout* (will.i.am and Britney Spears): falling in fourths back home.
- *Sir Duke* (Stevie Wonder): weak motion, a tritone leap.
- *Thank U, Next* (Ariana Grande): weak motion, G♭ to A.
- *Gangsta's Paradise* (Coolio): every function; a destination in position 4.

## Try this

Take a loop from [Tagg's tables](tagg-loops.qmd), write down the four motions as strong or weak, and name each
chord. Is it a cascade, a disc, or something else? Where is its destination?
